common_name: Texas Grano Onion (Classic Gulf South Short-Day Sweet Onion)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter zones; Texas Grano is a short-day onion requiring only 10-12 hours of daylight to bulb, making it well suited to fall planting and spring harvest in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens rather than a spring-planted crop as in the North.

directions: Start seeds indoors or direct-seed in the fall in mild-winter areas, since Texas Grano is a short-day type that needs the shorter daylight of southern winters to trigger bulbing rather than the long summer days farther north. Developed in Texas in the early 20th century, it became one of the foundational sweet onion cultivars of the Gulf South and is a direct ancestor of many modern short-day sweet onions, including some of the parent lines behind Vidalia-type onions. The large, globe-shaped bulbs have straw-yellow skin and mild, sweet flesh with low pungency, best used fresh rather than stored long term since sweet onions generally keep less well than pungent storage onions. Keep soil consistently moist through bulb formation and reduce water as tops begin to fall over before harvest.

common_name: White Bermuda Onion (Classic Mild Flat Short-Day Onion)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter zones; White Bermuda is a short-day type well suited to fall planting in the Gulf South, producing flattened bulbs with thin, papery white skin and very mild flesh.

directions: Start seeds indoors or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter regions, since this classic short-day onion needs the shorter daylight of a southern winter to bulb properly. Long grown in Texas, Louisiana, and other Gulf Coast states before more modern hybrid sweet onions became common, White Bermuda produces flattened, disc-shaped bulbs with thin, pure white skin and mild, tender flesh with relatively low pungency. Because the papery skin is thin, cured bulbs do not store as long as pungent storage onions and are best used within a few months of harvest. Keep soil evenly moist through bulb development and reduce watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall over ahead of harvest.

common_name: Evergreen Hardy White Bunching Onion (Cold-Hardy Perennial Scallion)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for a fall crop; this bunching onion does not form a bulb and is exceptionally cold-hardy, often overwintering in the ground to provide scallions the following spring even in fairly cold climates.

directions: Direct sow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike bulbing onions, this classic bunching onion (Welsh onion type) never forms a true bulb, instead producing clusters of straight, white-shanked scallions with mild, tender green tops. Its exceptional cold hardiness lets it overwinter in the ground in many climates, providing an extra-early harvest the following spring, and it can be cut back repeatedly through the growing season for a continuous supply. Because it multiplies by division at the base, an established clump can be divided every year or two to keep plantings vigorous and productive.

common_name: White Sweet Spanish Onion (Classic Long-Day Mild White Onion)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost and transplant after danger of hard frost has passed; White Sweet Spanish is a long-day type needing 14+ hours of summer daylight to bulb, making it best suited to northern and mid-latitude gardens rather than the short-day Gulf South.

directions: Start seeds indoors in late winter and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last hard frost. This long-established long-day onion produces large, globe-shaped bulbs with clean white skin and mild, juicy, sweet flesh with a milder bite than most storage onions, making it a popular choice for fresh eating, salads, and onion rings. Because long-day onions need the extended summer daylight of higher latitudes to bulb properly, it performs best north of about zone 7 and tends to produce poorly or bolt in the short-day Deep South. Keep soil consistently moist through bulb development and cure bulbs in a warm, airy spot after the tops fall over, though sweet types like this one store for a shorter time than pungent storage onions.

common_name: Borettana Cipollini Onion (Flat Golden Italian Onion)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in early spring; Borettana is an Italian heirloom cipollini type prized for its flat, disc-like shape that makes it ideal for whole-onion roasting and pickling.

directions: Direct sow or set transplants in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. This Italian heirloom produces distinctively flat, disc-shaped bulbs with coppery-gold skin and sweet, mild flesh, and is the classic cipollini used in Italian agrodolce (sweet-and-sour) roasted onion dishes as well as pickling, since the flat shape cooks evenly and looks attractive whole on the plate. It matures relatively quickly for an onion and the small-to-medium bulbs cure and store reasonably well for a sweet type. Space plants a bit closer than standard globe onions, since the flattened bulbs take up less lateral room, and reduce watering as the foliage begins to yellow and fall over near harvest.
